title: Biggest Land Mass
statement:
A map is a grid grid of 1 (land) and 0 (water). Land cells that share a side (up, down, left or right) belong to the same land mass; corner contact does not connect. The area of a mass is the number of land cells in it.

Return the area of the largest land mass, or 0 if there is no land.

examples.why: The masses have areas 3 (top left), 5 (the bent shape on the right) and 1 (bottom left). The answer is the largest area, not the number of masses (3) or the total land (9).
Every land cell touches the others only at corners, so each is its own mass of area 1. Counting diagonals would give 5.
No land, so the largest area is 0.

hints: This is counting land masses with one change: instead of counting how many floods you start, you measure how big each flood is.
Make the flood return or accumulate the number of cells it marks. Keep the maximum over all floods.
Use an explicit stack: push the start cell, and every time you pop a cell add one to the current area. Mark neighbours as seen when you push them so no cell is counted twice.

explain.intuition:
Each land mass is a connected group of cells, and a flood fill from any of its cells reaches exactly that group. So the plan is the same as counting masses: scan the grid, and when you find unvisited land, flood from it. The only new part is to count the cells as the flood visits them. Every cell is visited by exactly one flood, so the sizes are exact and the total work is one pass over the grid.

Depth-first fits naturally here because the answer is a sum over the cells reached, and the order does not matter. Use an explicit stack rather than recursion so a big mass does not overflow the call stack.
steps: When a cell is 1, set it to 0 (seen), push it, and set area = 0.
Pop cells until the stack is empty. For each popped cell add one to area, and push each in-bounds neighbour that is still 1, setting it to 0 as you push.
Update best = max(best, area) and continue the scan. Return best.
pitfalls: Counting a cell when it is pushed and again when it is popped, or marking it only on pop. A cell with two land neighbours can be pushed twice and the area comes out too large.
Returning the number of masses, or the total land. Example 1 has 3 masses and 9 land cells, but the answer is 5.
Recursive DFS on a 300 × 300 grid. One big mass is up to 90 000 nested calls, which exceeds Python's recursion limit. The recursive version below is only run on small grids.

complexity.space: O(rows · cols) for the stack in the worst case

solutions.title: Recursive DFS returning the area (small grids only)
solutions.idea: area(r, c) is 0 for water or out of bounds, otherwise 1 plus the area of the four neighbours after sinking this cell. Clear, but recursion depth can reach rows · cols.

solutions.title: Iterative DFS with a stack
solutions.idea: Flood each new mass with an explicit stack and count cells as they are popped. Each cell is pushed once, so the area is exact.

followups: You may turn exactly one water cell into land. What is the largest mass you can make? (Label each mass with an id and its size first.)
Return the cells of the biggest mass instead of its size. What changes?
